title: Patellar Tendinopathy
case: Case: A 25-year-old volleyball player has 4 months of pain just below the kneecap that is worse after training and with jumping. The lower pole of the patella is tender. A single-leg decline squat reproduces his pain at the tendon. Strength is good and there is no swelling or locking. He can extend the knee fully against gravity.

Working diagnosis: patellar tendinopathy. Plan: education, reduce jump volume, isometrics for pain, heavy slow leg press for about 12 weeks, add hip and calf strengthening, then plyometrics and sport drills.

differentials.name: Patellofemoral pain
differentials.key: Diffuse pain around or behind the patella, stairs and squats

differentials.name: Fat pad impingement
differentials.key: Pain beside the tendon, worse with full extension

differentials.name: Quadriceps tendinopathy
differentials.key: Pain at the upper pole of the patella

differentials.name: Osgood-Schlatter disease
differentials.key: Adolescent, pain and bump at the tibial tuberosity

differentials.name: Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease
differentials.key: Adolescent, pain at the lower pole of the patella

differentials.name: Partial tendon tear
differentials.key: Sudden severe pain in a previously painful tendon

differentials.name: Patellar tendon rupture
differentials.key: Cannot extend the knee, gap, high-riding patella

qa: Why use a decline squat? The decline position increases tendon load and reduces the contribution of other structures, so it helps reproduce tendon pain.
Why is deep friction not recommended? Evidence does not show lasting benefit, and tendon capacity is built by loading.
The patient says he felt a pop and cannot lift his straight leg. What now? Suspect complete rupture and refer urgently.
Why avoid steroid injection into the tendon? Because of the risk of tendon weakening and rupture.

How do you separate patellar tendinopathy from patellofemoral pain? Tendinopathy is a localised point of pain at the lower pole, triggered by jumping and tendon loading, while patellofemoral pain is more diffuse around or behind the kneecap and linked to squats, stairs and sitting.

tests.name: Palpation of the inferior pole of the patella

fields.Position: Supine with the knee extended and the quadriceps relaxed, or with the knee at about 30 degrees
fields.Action: Push the lower pole of the patella up slightly and press on the tendon attachment with the thumb. Compare with the other side
fields.Positive: Localised tenderness at the lower pole of the patella that reproduces the familiar pain
fields.Supports: Patellar tendinopathy when combined with the history
fields.Limits: Fat pad irritation, the patellofemoral joint and other structures may also be tender, so interpret with the loading tests

fields.Purpose: Load the patellar tendon more than the patellofemoral joint to reproduce the familiar pain
fields.Position: Standing on one leg on a decline board of about 25 degrees (a firm sloped surface), with the heel raised so that the shin is steep
fields.Action: Slowly squat on one leg to about 60 degrees of knee bend and return, repeating several times; ask about the location and level of pain
fields.Positive: Reproduction of the familiar pain at the tendon, particularly at the lower pole of the patella
fields.Supports: Patellar tendinopathy; pain behind or around the kneecap more suggests patellofemoral pain
fields.Limits: Not specific; the decline angle and depth change the load
fields.Next step: Use the test and pain score as a baseline to follow the response to treatment

fields.Action: Ask the patient to straighten the knee against gravity and to do a straight leg raise. Palpate for a gap at the tendon and look for a high-riding patella
fields.Positive: The patient cannot extend the knee against gravity, or a gap is felt

redFlags.Finding: Sudden pop and inability to straighten the knee against gravity, palpable gap, high-riding patella
Recent steroid injection or fluoroquinolone use with new severe pain
Hot red swollen knee with fever
Constant night pain, weight loss, a lump
Adolescent knee pain with a limp and limited hip rotation
redFlags.Why it matters: Hip problem referred to the knee

manual.name: Soft-tissue work for the quadriceps, hamstrings, calf

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education and progressive loading. Manual therapy is a minor adjunct. Do not claim that manual therapy repairs the tendon or breaks down scar tissue.

exercise.Exercise: Isometric knee extension or wall sit with the knee at about 60 degrees
exercise.Starting dose: 5 holds of 30 to 45 seconds, once or twice a day

exercise.Exercise: Leg press, hack squat or squat
exercise.Starting dose: 3 sets of 15, then reduce to 12, 10, 8 repetitions as load increases; 3 days a week for about 12 weeks
exercise.Progress when: Good control and no next-day flare

exercise.Exercise: Hopping, skipping, pogo jumps, then jumping and landing
exercise.Progress when: Pain stays under about 4 out of 10

exerciseNotes: Principle: progressive loading of the patellar tendon is first-line. A staged approach is often used: pain relief with isometrics, then building strength with heavy slow resistance, then energy storage (jumping and landing), then sport-specific work. Pain up to about 4 out of 10 during exercise is generally acceptable if it settles within 24 hours and the tendon is not worse the next morning.

Supporting exercises: hip and calf strengthening (bridge, calf raise), trunk control, and landing technique practice. Landing mechanics training may reduce load on the tendon, but evidence is limited.

Load management: reduce, rather than stop, jumping and sprinting load until pain settles. Keep a log of volume, intensity and pain. In-season, isometrics may reduce pain for a short time and allow play, but this effect is temporary.

Return to sport criteria (example): pain at or below a low level during sport drills, VISA-P improving, good single-leg strength and landing control, and tolerance of jumping volume. No fixed date is given.

modalities.name: Extracorporeal shockwave
modalities.indicated: Option for persistent pain after several months of loading

modalities.name: Patellar tendon strap
modalities.comment: May reduce pain during activity; limited evidence

modalityNotes: Medical options (decided by doctors): corticosteroid injection into the tendon is generally avoided because of the rupture risk. Other injections and surgery are for persistent cases after months of non-surgical care.
pathway: Any emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.
Cannot extend the knee or a palpable gap? Yes: urgent referral.
Pain localised to the lower pole of the patella, load-related, reproduced by a single-leg decline squat, and no other cause? Yes: working diagnosis is patellar tendinopathy.
Diffuse anterior pain and stair or sitting provocation? Use the patellofemoral pain pathway.
Begin load management and a progressive loading program. Adjust for sport timing and season.
If there is no improvement after a full course of consistent loading, review the diagnosis and consider specialist options.
Visit 1: screen for rupture and other flags, explain tendinopathy as a load problem, set goals and timeline.
Early: manage jumping load, begin isometrics if painful.
